analysis.one_liner: Gives states sole authority to regulate fracking, stripping federal rules even on federal land.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in four House committees for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would hand each state the only power to write and enforce rules on hydraulic fracturing — fracking — within its borders, including fracking done on national forests, public lands, and other federal land inside that state. It would remove the Bureau of Land Management's role in setting federal fracking standards for federal land. The bill was referred to four House committees and never moved; no hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred, and the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land, which would face one state rulebook instead of federal standards set by the Bureau of Land Management. States with large oil and gas industries would gain full control over fracking rules on all land within their borders, including land owned by all Americans. Geothermal developers are also covered by the bill's definition and would benefit similarly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies drilling federal land

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives states the sole authority to write and enforce any regulation, guidance, or permit requirement for hydraulic fracturing within their boundaries, eliminating overlapping federal permitting [S2].
It specifically subjects fracking on federal land — public lands, National Forest land, Bureau of Reclamation land, and Corps of Engineers land — to state law rather than federal regulation [S3].

The bill's findings section argues that states already have comprehensive, effective oil and gas regulations and cites studies and testimony saying there is no proven case of groundwater contamination from the fracking process itself [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who live near or use federal lands — including national forests and Bureau of Land Management property — would lose a uniform federal floor for fracking on that land, and would depend entirely on the rules of whichever state they live in. Water users downstream of federal-land drilling would rely on state standards that vary widely from state to state. Taxpayers collectively own the federal land in question, and the bill removes the federal government's say over drilling on it.

drawbacks.text: Fracking on federal land would no longer answer to federal standards, so a company drilling in a national forest would follow only that state's rules; states differ sharply in well-construction, chemical disclosure, and wastewater requirements, and states collecting drilling revenue face pressure to keep rules light [S3].

Federal land belongs to all Americans, not just residents of the state where it sits; the bill would let a single state's rules govern drilling on land the whole public owns, removing any national standard [S2].

The bill's own text concedes that related activity — surface discharges, wastewater disposal, and air emissions — is federally regulated under existing environmental statutes, but it would carve the fracking process itself out of federal oversight even on federal land, leaving a patchwork for the practice most associated with water-quality concerns [S3].
An honest supporter would acknowledge that some state oil and gas agencies are small and industry-funded, so quality of oversight would depend on geography rather than a consistent national baseline.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For drillers, the benefit is real and immediate: one state rulebook instead of federal permitting, faster permits, and no national floor. For the public, the cost is that the frack jobs on federally owned land would be governed only by the state where the land sits — a state that often receives the drilling revenue — with no uniform federal protection for groundwater, disclosure, or well integrity on land all taxpayers own. The bill cites state and industry-backed studies to argue state rules are adequate, but those are contested findings and the federal land issue is the part of the bill with the clearest one-way transfer: industry gains flexibility, the public co-owners of the land lose a layer of oversight.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees when introduced in February 2017, bounced among four subcommittees, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Representative Louie Gohmert introduced the bill on February 7, 2017, with six Republican cosponsors: Representatives Steve King of Iowa, Ted Yoho, Tom Cole, Steve Pearce, and Kevin Cramer [S1].

On introduction it was referred to the Natural Resources, Agriculture, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Energy and Commerce committees, with the Speaker to decide later which committee would lead [S5].

Within three weeks in February 2017 it was sent to four subcommittees — Water Resources and Environment, Environment, Energy and Mineral Resources, and Conservation and Forestry — and no further action was recorded for the rest of the 115th Congress [S5].
No committee ever reported the bill, no version was introduced in the Senate in the record provided, and no vote of any kind took place [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The outcome left the existing system in place: the Bureau of Land Management retains authority over fracking standards on federal land and states keep their existing rules without the bill's carve-out. Oil and gas companies drilling federal land did not get the single state-rulebook regime they would have gained had it passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public co-owners of federal land, for now

industries.industry: Oil and gas drillers on federal land
industries.note: The bill would give drillers a single state rulebook instead of Bureau of Land Management fracking standards on federal land, cutting permit costs and removing a national floor on well rules. The public co-owns that land, so the industry's gain comes directly at the expense of a layer of public oversight.

The bill's definition covers fluids used to enhance geothermal production, so geothermal developers would get the same state-only permitting relief. Their operations share the drillers' interest in fewer overlapping rules.

State agencies would become the sole regulator of fracking within their borders, including on federal land, expanding their authority. But states with large drilling industries also collect drilling revenue, which can pull oversight toward the industry being regulated.
